edges.effect_quant: In a prospective Italian multicenter study of 5416 IBD outpatients, anemia prevalence was 13.6% and 62.5% of anemia cases were driven by iron deficiency; in a Dutch multicenter cohort of 2197 outpatients, anemia occurred in 18.0%, iron deficiency in 43.4%, and iron-deficiency anemia in 12.2%.
edges.population: adults with Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, or IBD-unclassified
edges.mechanism: Inflammatory bowel disease promotes chronic intestinal blood loss, reduced intake, impaired absorption, and hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration. These pathways often coexist, making iron deficiency anemia one of the most common systemic complications of active IBD.
edges.summary: Inflammatory bowel disease is strongly linked to iron deficiency anemia, with iron deficiency accounting for most anemia seen in outpatient cohorts. The relationship is clinically important because it worsens fatigue and quality of life, yet remains undertreated in a substantial fraction of patients.
edges.caveats: The exact prevalence varies with disease activity, ferritin definitions, and how rigorously iron studies are measured. Some patients have mixed anemia from inflammation plus iron deficiency, so ferritin alone can underestimate the problem during flares.
